h: A resignation is not enough: free the watchdog institutions from the government
dek: Law professor Tarunabh Khaitan says Gyanesh Kumar must go, but the real cure is a new, multi-party framework for appointing constitutional bodies and holding them to account.
body: The Constitution promises free and fair elections, and guarding that promise is the job of the Election Commission. Tarunabh Khaitan, who teaches public law at the London School of Economics, recalls that according to an Indian Express investigation, two of the three election commissioners recorded written objections to SIR-related decisions at least 14 times in ten months, and even called some decisions illegal. The Commission's reply was that the decisions were unanimous. Khaitan says that at first sight it seems Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar was hollowing out his duty instead of doing it.

He demands that Kumar resign and that there be an inquiry under the electoral integrity provisions of the Representation of the People Act 1950 and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (the new criminal code). The obstacle is the 2023 law that governs how commissioners are appointed. One of its sections protects both serving and former office holders from prosecution, which the writer considers probably unconstitutional.

But the real thrust of the piece is that removing one man is not enough. A democracy is one in which parties lose elections; governments come and go, the state endures. To protect this difference, constitutional watchdogs such as judges, election and information commissioners, the Lokpal (anti-corruption ombudsman), governors and police chiefs need an independent framework for appointment and accountability. Otherwise every guarantee depends on the goodwill of those in power.

In 2019 Khaitan had put forward the outline of an Independent Institutions Bill. A parliamentary committee would have two members from the government side and one each from the three largest opposition parties, so that a united opposition could stop the government. Sri Lanka's Constitutional Council is one such example.

For this he lists ten principles: no one-sided appointments, a role for the Rajya Sabha and the states, fixed terms, an independent inquiry before removal, collective decisions in multi-member bodies, a bar on government posts after retirement, and annual public hearings. Posts such as governor may also need a constitutional amendment.

In the end he writes that the small wounds inflicted on the Constitution in Modi's first term have now grown deeper and more numerous. The Cockroach Janta Party movement is a moment of reckoning. The government may save itself by sacrificing a minister or an official; the question must be asked whether it can also be forced to repair a broken system.
nazar: Khaitan is saying what street slogans often miss. Even if Gyanesh Kumar left tomorrow, the 2023 law would stay as it is, under which the Prime Minister and a minister of his choice together pick the next commissioner. The face would change, the key would stay in the same hand. So the demands at Jantar Mantar must include changing the appointment law alongside the resignation. That is the real test.

For us this is not a matter of academic debate. When watchdog institutions are in the pocket of power, the first to lose their rights are those without lawyers, papers or influence: Dalits, Adivasis (indigenous communities), Muslims, migrant workers and women. Independent institutions are the shield of these very people, and this movement has to become a demand for that shield.
sawal: If the face changes but the key stays in the same hand, what has changed?
ref: Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023

This law removed the Chief Justice of India from the committee that selects commissioners and put in a Union minister chosen by the Prime Minister. It also gives immunity from prosecution for decisions taken in office.
Special Intensive Revision (SIR)
An Election Commission drive in which voter rolls were checked afresh. Critics say the names of a large number of genuine voters were struck off in it.
ank: written objections by two commissioners in ten months
principles for a law on independent institutions

h: From Boat Club to Jantar Mantar, and now out of the city?
dek: Dilip Khan recalls how protest in Delhi has been pushed further from power every time, and asks what a protest is worth if no one is made to hear it.
body: The piece opens hundreds of kilometres from Delhi. At Itarsi station police took fifteen young people linked to the Cockroach Janta Party off a Delhi-bound train. Similar stops were reported from Pune, Bhopal and Gwalior. The organisation claims more than ten thousand detentions, a figure neither confirmed nor denied.

In Delhi, meanwhile: a request to shut 57 metro stations, trains to New Delhi and Nizamuddin cancelled for ten hours, the BSF and thousands of personnel at the borders. The police cite a late application and the July march. To the writer, these arguments reveal panic more than strength.

The sharpest point comes from the Supreme Court hearing. The court said the metro should not be shut completely, but in the same breath suggested the government find a venue other than Jantar Mantar, which the government accepted at once. The writer sees it as opening the door with one hand and removing the destination with the other.

He recalls the history: after Tikait's farmers in 1988, protests at Boat Club were stopped and dissent was pushed to Jantar Mantar. In 2017 that too was banned, until the Supreme Court lifted the ban in 2018. The whole point of protest is that power hears it. A ground in some corner of the city grants permission but takes away the purpose.

Finally the piece takes the question to its root. This movement is not about a minister but about the accountability of the institution on whose credibility the government's own legitimacy rests. Drawing on Hannah Arendt, he argues that the more police there are, the less confidence power has. And he recalls Lohia's line that living nations do not wait five years, a line the BJP repeated often while in opposition.
nazar: This is the most urgent question of the day, because the fight is no longer only over Gyanesh Kumar's chair but over the place from which the public can call out to power. Jantar Mantar is not a building but a right: any citizen from far away, a Dalit family, a group of Adivasis, can carry their words to the ears of Parliament.

Sending protest out of the city means giving it a ground full of facilities but deaf. The question of those fifteen young people taken off the train is exactly this: if the vote itself is in doubt and the road is closed too, which door is left for the citizen?
sawal: If power cannot hear a protest, is it still a protest?
ref: Boat Club, 1988
The ground near India Gate where lakhs of farmers led by Mahendra Singh Tikait camped. Protests there were banned afterwards.
Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan case
The Supreme Court's 2018 ruling that lifted the blanket ban on protests at Jantar Mantar and held that the right to protest cannot be extinguished.

h: Gyaneshgate: is this about to become Modi's Watergate?
dek: Journalists Sunil Gatade and Venkatesh Kesari argue that the storm over the Chief Election Commissioner is now reaching the credibility of the government itself.
body: According to the writers, 2 October was different this time. After 2014 Gandhi had largely been reduced to Swachh Bharat (the Clean India campaign), but on this Gandhi Jayanti the opposition turned its own cleanliness drive towards the Election Commission and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. At Jantar Mantar and at Shivaji Park in Mumbai there were calls for his removal, and on 6 October a march to the Commission's office was led by Rahul Gandhi and John Brittas.

The opposition wants to make this Modi's Watergate, the scandal that forced Nixon to resign. Its argument is that if the disputed decisions were Kumar's alone and not the whole Commission's, then the very basis for trusting recent elections is shaken. The writers say people have come to believe that the elections in Maharashtra, Delhi, Bihar and Bengal were managed; this is an allegation, not a proven fact.

According to the writers, before this post Kumar was seen as very close to Amit Shah. A former chief secretary of Kerala claims that Kumar had offered him a BJP ticket. There is also the charge that, relying on the immunity in the 2023 law, he ignored the objections. An attempt to show all was well through a meeting with fellow commissioners Sandhu and Joshi ended up confirming their objections instead.

Modi and Shah are silent so far. Some BJP chief ministers have come out in his defence, while senior ministers stay on the sidelines. The writers point out that Dharmendra Pradhan had to go under public pressure; if Kumar does not go either, he will remain the government's weak spot.

There are several petitions in the courts, but the Cockroach Janta Party says the reckoning will not be left to the courts. According to the writers, the courts did not stop the SIR even when names were struck off in huge numbers. The opposition claims that 13 crore (130 million) names were removed, and demands that the SIR be stopped at once and that those whose votes were taken away get justice.
nazar: The Watergate comparison has weight, but one difference must be kept in mind. Nixon fell because newspapers dug, a court ordered the tapes and Congress prepared for impeachment. Here those same institutions either stayed silent or woke up late, and the burden has fallen on the street. So rather than leaving the allegations as allegations, the most important demand is an independent, time-bound inquiry, so that the truth comes out on paper and not in slogans.

And if the opposition's figure of 13 crore is even half right, this would be the biggest disenfranchisement in history. It would have hit hardest those who live in rented rooms, move between cities, or whose names are spelt differently in government records.
sawal: Who will count the people whose names were struck off?
ref: Watergate (1972-74)

A scandal in the United States over a break-in at the office of the opposition Democratic Party and the cover-up that followed. The investigation reached President Nixon, and in 1974 he had to resign.
Approver
A person involved in a crime who agrees to testify against the other accused, usually in return for a pardon or leniency.

h: A cockroach democracy, born of a judge's remark
dek: Recording July's march to Parliament, Arundhati Roy writes that unarmed young people have broken the climate of fear, but that without political work this anger could also scatter.
body: Arundhati Roy says that after years of despair she has once again felt proud to be Indian. According to reports, Chief Justice Surya Kant had called some unemployed young people cockroaches and parasites. Abhijeet Dipke, a student in Boston, tweeted asking what would happen if all the cockroaches united; lakhs of people joined in, and the Cockroach Janta Party was born. Its first demand was the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

In the background are paper leaks. According to the opposition, there have been about 152 paper leaks since 2014, and after the NEET leak in May at least 12 students took their own lives. On 6 June Sonam Wangchuk began an indefinite fast at Jantar Mantar; on 18 July the police forcibly carried him off the stage.

On 20 July, the day of the march to Parliament, thousands arrived by train, bus and metro. The police closed roads and metro stations, tried to cut the internet, welded barricades shut, and used batons and tear gas. According to Roy, people of every religion and caste shielded one another from the police, and jokes and memes broke the poisonous fear that had become normal.

At first Roy feared it might turn out like the Anna movement of 2011. What took her to Jantar Mantar was the media's hostility and Dipke's remark that had they been Muslims, they would be in jail. Umar Khalid has been in jail for almost six years without trial. Roy is also troubled by the relief that most protesters were Hindu, because had they been Muslim, Sikh, Christian or Adivasi (indigenous), they would have been crushed.

In the bigger picture she calls the SIR a return of the CAA-NRC, with lakhs of names being cut from the voter rolls, and alleges that the government's confidence comes from its capture of the election machinery. Her warning is that if the opposition does not unite and do political work, this anger will cool, and that those in power will not hesitate even at bloodshed.
nazar: Written in July, this piece rings even truer today. On 2 October people at Jantar Mantar were packed into buses, and before 10 October permission was refused, metro stations were shut and trains to Delhi were cancelled. A government that blocks the way to the very place of protest is revealing its own weakness.

Roy's bitterest point is the most necessary one: the leeway this movement has received was never given to Muslims, Adivasis and Kashmiris. The real test of the Cockroach Janta Party will be whether it stands just as firmly with Umar Khalid and with the voters whose names are being quietly removed from the rolls.
sawal: If these cockroaches had been Muslims, would they have survived on the street?
ref: Umar Khalid

A JNU research scholar arrested under the UAPA (anti-terror law) in the case of an alleged conspiracy behind the 2020 Delhi riots. Several bail pleas have been rejected, and the trial has still not begun.
Anna movement (2011)
Anna Hazare's movement against corruption and for a Lokpal (anti-corruption ombudsman). Many critics, Roy among them, believe its political benefit finally went to the BJP.

h: The shuttered Supreme Court station: how far does a court's order reach?
dek: Senior advocate Sanjay Hegde asks how a court that cannot get a metro station bearing its own name reopened will protect citizens' freedoms.
body: Hegde begins in 1975, when during the Emergency the Times of India carried an obituary saying that a gentleman named D'Ocracy had passed away on 26 June. The censors missed it, the readers understood. Fifty years later, a cartoon by Rohit Kumar for The Wire shows a map of a people's metro whose closed stations are democracy, expression, free media, the right to protest, secularism, equality and fraternity. One station was left out, says Hegde: the Supreme Court.

On 22 July, during the Cockroach Janta Party protest at Jantar Mantar, sixteen metro stations were closed in the name of security. The Supreme Court station on the Blue Line, which takes people to the court and to lawyers' chambers, was kept shut on police advice so that protesters could not walk from there to Jantar Mantar. The blow fell on litigants, clerks and young lawyers. The president of the Bar Association raised the matter, the Chief Justice made a promise, and still the station stayed shut.

The writer points to Article 144 of the Constitution, under which all civil and judicial authorities in the country shall act in aid of the Supreme Court, the Delhi Police and the Metro corporation included. If a station bearing the court's name does not open at the court's word, its authority is in question.

He gives examples from the United States. In 1957 in Little Rock, when the governor stopped nine Black students from entering a school, President Eisenhower sent troops to get them admitted, and the next year the court said its interpretation applied to every governor. In 1962 James Meredith was escorted by marshals to the University of Mississippi. There the court did not plead for help; it demanded it and got it.

On the other side is the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II, who was left with titles but no power to enforce his orders. Hegde's conclusion is that the rule of law exists only when a court gives an order and the government enforces it equally on everyone. A court's order should first reach the station that bears its name.
nazar: In July sixteen stations were closed; this time 57 stations were ordered shut and trains to Delhi were cancelled. On 9 October the Supreme Court said the metro cannot be shut down completely. Hegde's question is now the direct test for tomorrow: will this order be carried out on the ground, or will police advice once again outweigh a court's order?

Shutting the metro is less a way of stopping protesters and more a way of punishing the whole city. Patients going to hospital, daily wage workers, women who work in homes and students who have come from far away all get stuck that day. For a government that wants to silence its own citizens by blocking their way, the words undeclared emergency do not seem too heavy.
sawal: Tomorrow, will the court's order prevail, or the police's advice?
ref: Article 144
A provision of the Constitution saying that all civil and judicial authorities in the country shall act in aid of the Supreme Court. In other words, enforcing the court's orders is their duty.
Cooper v. Aaron (1958)
A US Supreme Court ruling signed by all nine judges. It said the court's interpretation of the Constitution is binding on the governor and legislature of every state.

h: Barricades at Jantar Mantar: the country is not the rulers' private estate
dek: Using the police action of 2 October, Sanjay K. Jha asks whether democracy means ruling by decree or the rights of citizens, and demands that the Prime Minister remove Gyanesh Kumar.
body: On Gandhi Jayanti, 2 October, several organisations wanted to gather at Jantar Mantar. The demand was that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resign over the allegations of irregularities in the SIR. Sanjay K. Jha writes that the police got nearby metro stations closed, put up several layers of barricades, and quickly packed students, activists and leaders into buses. MP Manoj Jha, Yogendra Yadav and Neha Bora of AISA were detained.

Jha says democracy has now become a cover for the rulers' decrees and police power. The Prime Minister and ministers are not the owners of this country. He compares the Prime Minister's plane costing 8,400 crore, his car costing 12 crore and his daily security costing 1.6 crore with an ordinary citizen who cannot even reach the protest site. Demonetisation and the Covid lockdown were also decisions taken without asking the people.

The piece recalls that Gyanesh Kumar faces allegations of vote theft and of cutting 13 crore names. Jha asks who is a strong leader: one who suppresses the truth, sets agencies on critics and runs on propaganda is in fact weak. If faith in elections is to be restored, Modi should cut himself loose from Gyanesh Kumar.

The voices from the protest are the liveliest part of the piece. An elderly woman refused to leave without seeing Neha Bora. Some policemen admitted in private that a peaceful protest should have been allowed and that senior officers were acting on the signals of their political masters. One veteran activist did not come at all, out of fear of police violence.

Jha's conclusion is that if the repression continues, the BJP will pay for it, because voters are moving beyond nationalism, promises of development postponed to 2047, and polarisation. The government should choose accountability, not force.
nazar: 2 October was a rehearsal. On 10 October permission was not given at all, 57 metro stations were ordered shut and trains to Delhi were cancelled. The veteran activist who stayed home out of fear is the truest measure of this period. If even the designated place for protest is closed in a democracy, what is left?

But demanding the sacrifice of one officer is not enough. The 2023 law removed the Chief Justice from the committee that picks election commissioners and gave the government a majority. Until this appointment structure changes, Gyanesh Kumar will be replaced by another Gyanesh Kumar.
sawal: Why the ban even where protest is permitted?
ref: Jantar Mantar

An area near Parliament that has for decades been Delhi's designated protest site. In 2017 the NGT (National Green Tribunal) stopped protests here; in 2018 the Supreme Court restored permission with rules.
Chief Election Commissioner appointment law, 2023
This law put a Union minister in place of the Chief Justice on the selection committee. The committee now has the Prime Minister, a minister and the Leader of the Opposition.

h: Caught in a lie: will Gyanesh Kumar now be held to account?
dek: Maneesh Chhibber writes that the Supreme Court has finally shown some firmness with the Election Commission, but that this is not enough to restore trust.
body: For about a year the Supreme Court kept accepting the Election Commission's argument that the Special Intensive Revision of the voter rolls, the SIR, was proper and transparent. According to Maneesh Chhibber, after recent investigations by a section of the press and large protests, the court's patience now seems to have run out.

A bench led by Chief Justice Surya Kant issued notices to the Commission on petitions seeking action over Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's one-sided way of working, including sidelining the other two commissioners. The court also made clear that it had not approved any change to Form 6, used to register new voters.

This clarification matters, because in a press release on 26 September the Commission had said that the declaration attached to Form 6 for the SIR carried the Supreme Court's seal of approval. The writer calls this claim false and says that by making such a claim about court proceedings, Kumar and the Commission's officials could come within the scope of perjury. He also complains that the court should have voiced its displeasure in stronger words, especially since it was the court itself that had given the Commission almost a free hand on the SIR.

The piece also cites reports that election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi recorded at least 14 objections to SIR-related decisions in the past ten months. Some orders were issued without their knowledge or advice. The two also wrote to Cabinet Secretary T V Somanathan raising concerns about the reliability of the voter software.

Chhibber sees this as a turning point, but with a warning. If the court does not take concrete steps to restore people's trust in the voter rolls, it too may be seen as an equal partner in what the Commission has done.
nazar: Form 6 is not a technical paper; it is the door through which a new voter enters democracy. If conditions the court never approved are added at that door, and then justified in the court's name, the first to be left out are those without full papers: young first-time voters, migrant workers, Adivasis (indigenous communities), the homeless, and women who move house after marriage.

The court's belated firmness is welcome, but a notice is not justice. Without a deadline for restoring the names that were cut, or never allowed to be added, in the meantime, this correction will remain incomplete.
sawal: A lie told in the court's name: who will be punished for it?
ref: Form 6
The Election Commission form through which a new voter, or a person who has moved to another constituency, applies to have their name entered in the voter roll.
Perjury
Knowingly making a false statement in court or in a matter connected with court proceedings. It is a punishable offence under Indian law.

h: Gyanesh babu, on the road to immortality through abuse
dek: In this satire by Vishnu Nagar, the Chief Election Commissioner is a trapped man who hears abuse every day but consoles himself that history will remember him alongside Modi and Shah.
body: Vishnu Nagar's Gyanesh Kumar is in deep trouble. If he resigns, he fears Modi and Shah will frame him in some case so the secrets do not come out. If he stays, he hears thief, bandit and traitor every day, there are calls for his arrest, and Rahul Gandhi separately warns him to turn approver or face jail if the government changes. On top of that comes the advice from above: take the abuse quietly, we hear it every day too, and look how healthy we are.

Nagar works out that had he been an ordinary corrupt IAS officer, he would have retired to a bungalow in Gurugram, faced at most one tax raid and then got bail. But our hero, according to the satire, drafted the removal of Article 370, lent a hand in the Ram temple trust, and in the end wiped 13 crore names off the voter rolls.

The plan ahead was settled too: first the Rajya Sabha, then a ministry, then a governorship in some opposition-ruled state to get in its way, and finally Vice President or President, where he would sign whatever paper came his way.

But the real consolation lies elsewhere. Infamy too is, after all, a kind of immortality. Gen Z and Gen Alpha will remember him along with Modi and Shah, while Rajnath Singh, Shivraj Singh Chouhan and even his predecessor Rajiv Kumar will be forgotten.

And why do the rulers need him? Nagar counts it out: 2014 was won with lies, 2019 with hate, but in 2024 the vehicle got stuck at about 240 seats. Hindutva, Sanatan, the Ram temple, Pulwama, rhetoric against Muslims, free rations, mocking nicknames for opponents, breaking parties and buying MPs, all of it has been tried. All that is left is the voter roll. At the end comes the writer's mock sympathy: nobody understands the poor man's helplessness.
nazar: Satire is sharpest when its foundation is no joke. The written dissent of two election commissioners, lakhs of names cut, and the barricades at Jantar Mantar are not imagination. Nagar puts a layer of laughter over these very facts, and the layer stings because the wound beneath it is real.

When people start openly laughing at the head of an institution, the damage to its credibility goes deeper than any court ruling. Laughter is the opposite of fear, and the young people on the streets are using exactly this weapon.
sawal: How can elections be run under an officer the country laughs at?
ref: Rajiv Kumar
Chief Election Commissioner before Gyanesh Kumar, under whose watch the 2024 Lok Sabha election was held. He retired in February 2025.
Approver
An accused person who agrees to testify against their associates in return for a pardon.

h: The Commission's correction drive, or a confession of error?
dek: An analysis in The Wire alleges that the Election Commission's latest instructions themselves admit that legitimate voters were cut in the SIR, and that the burden is now being put on those same voters.
body: After a meeting of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar with commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, the Commission told every state to run a special drive for voters left out in or after the SIR. Officials are to compare the old and new rolls, visit the homes of voters who were cut, and get Form 6 filled. The analysis calls this a confession made under compulsion: if only dead, duplicate or departed voters had been removed, why this drive?

Form 6 is meant for new voters, but people already registered are having to come back as new applicants. According to the piece, a mandatory declaration linking Form 6 on ECINET to the old SIR roll was added without changing the 1960 rules. The two dissenting commissioners had raised this; now the Commission is bringing back the old form outside the SIR.

The charge is that software took the place of law. In Goa officials found 97 voters to be genuine, but despite eight warnings ECINET had no way to restore them, and now an IIT committee will look into it. The Supreme Court handed the decision on about 60 lakh doubtful voters to judicial officers, yet 16.10 lakh appeals were filed through the central system in Delhi against restored voters. Who filed them is not clear.

The charges about Form 7 are the most serious. In Dhamnagar in Odisha about 3,200 applications came in to cut names, more than 90 percent of them of Muslims, and an assistant officer was suspended. In Babaleshwar in Karnataka, 1,363 of 1,373 applications were filed by ten people, and in Haridwar 1,657 of 4,099 objections came from 35 names, 31 of them BJP booth agents. Several cases are under investigation.

The analysis says the annual registration of new voters has been stalled since 2024 and young people's names have not been added in at least 16 states. It asks for court intervention and puts the political accountability on the Prime Minister.
nazar: There is a clear map in these figures. Among those whose names were cut, a large number are Muslims, poor migrants and people without papers, and those whose names are not being added are the very young people who are on the streets today. The 10 October march is against this double blow.

If the Commission really wants to correct things, it should first say who filed the 16 lakh appeals, how many people faced action over fake Form 7s, and why the dissent of its own two commissioners was ignored. Admitting a mistake and dodging accountability cannot go together.
sawal: Who filed sixteen lakh appeals, and in whose names?
ref: Form 6 and Form 7
Form 6 is the application to add a new name to the voter roll. Form 7 is for objecting to a name and having it removed, for example on grounds of death or duplicate registration.
ECINET
The Election Commission's central online platform, through which voter roll applications and decisions run. The charge is that it overrode the legal powers of officers on the ground.

h: Gen Z is not praying, it is fighting for democracy
dek: Brown University political scientist Ashutosh Varshney argues that the students' movement against the voter rolls is not a party fight but a response to the biggest assault on Indian democracy since the Emergency.
body: Ashutosh Varshney's first request is that the young people who have come out at Jantar Mantar and across the country not be seen through the lens of everyday party politics. In his view they are standing up against what should be called the biggest assault on Indian democracy since the Emergency of 1975-77. Rahul Gandhi is a party leader making use of this mood; the movement is bigger than him.

He then recalls an old puzzle: in a poor, barely industrialised India, democracy survived, contrary to the theories of scholars. Varshney distinguishes between electoral democracy and liberal democracy: elections continuing to be held is one thing, protecting free speech, civil society and minority rights is another. In his view, after 2014 the liberal part weakened, while the electoral part stayed more or less strong.

The most important part of the piece is that after 2024 the electoral part too began to wobble, and he sees the root of this in the SIR. As he sees it, the SIR rests on two ideas: to be a voter you need full papers, and the responsibility for getting a name registered lies with the citizen, not the state. The makers of the Constitution thought the opposite, that it was the state's duty to reach the poor and less educated and register their names. Now papers are being demanded, and those with the fewest papers are the poor.

Varshney links this to voter suppression in the United States, where paperwork requirements hit Black voters first and now poor Hispanic voters. V-Dem counts the US too among declining democracies; India is not alone.

At the end he recalls the dawn of Sahir Ludhianvi's songs, which the characters in his films awaited in prayer. Today's generation, in his words, is not praying but fighting without fear. What the result will be, change or more repression, he does not know, but he says that it no longer looks easy for the government to halt its slipping grip.
nazar: The value of this piece is that it ties the demand for Gyanesh Kumar's resignation to a larger question: must the citizen prove the right to vote, or will the state deliver it? This very difference becomes the gulf between a voter in a settlement like Bela Estate and a voter in a posh colony. If the movement stops at one officer's chair, this real question will once again be buried in files.
sawal: Should the citizen prove they are a voter, or should the state find them?
ref: V-Dem
A project of the University of Gothenburg in Sweden that measures the health of democracies around the world every year. For some years it has placed India in the category of electoral autocracy.
Voter suppression
A term used in the United States for keeping certain groups away from the vote through methods such as ID requirements, strict registration rules and purging names.

h: From across the border: with Modi, anything is possible, now in reverse
dek: According to well-known Pakistani columnist Wusatullah Khan, the alleged theft of a few crore votes could prove the final crack in the trust on which twelve years of power have rested.
body: Wusatullah Khan opens his column with the slogan on which the BJP has fought three elections since 2014. He says that twelve years on, the corruption, disregard for law and bullying hidden behind this slogan are now plainly visible, and that this has been done by a generation the government never took seriously.

The story runs from last July, when exam papers leaked and, under pressure from young people, Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan had to go. The writer guesses the government must have thought the anger would now cool. Then came the Indian Express report, according to which Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar had names cut in huge numbers during the scrutiny of the voter rolls, despite objections from two members of the Commission. The writer alleges that most of them were Muslims and Hindus seen as opponents of the BJP.

The young people came out on the streets again and the major opposition parties stood with them. Khan pauses on one image: on 2 October, while the Prime Minister was paying tribute to Gandhi, in the same city the police were wielding batons on protesters at Jantar Mantar.

The column does not see this as a single event. A rape charge against men in uniform involving a minor in Delhi, an IIT student's suicide linked to caste harassment, a results scam in Pune: the writer says that when the road to change looks closed, even a small spark becomes a fire. Demonetisation, unemployment, farmers, Kashmir, public assets going to billionaires: the list of things people have endured is long.

His conclusion is that the BJP is not sinking suddenly, but the captain's hand is slipping from the rudder. The high of the politics of hate comes on fast and wears off just as fast, and crores of stolen votes, if the allegations are true, could prove the last straw.
nazar: This column from across the border is interesting because it shows that the batons at Jantar Mantar are now shaping the image of Indian democracy in the neighbourhood too. Many of Khan's points are allegations and guesses, and the religious breakdown of the cut names has not yet been established by any inquiry. But his basic point is right: the real capital of power is trust, and trust begins with the voter roll.
sawal: When a neighbour pities our elections, whose shame is it?
ref: Wusatullah Khan
A senior journalist and columnist from Karachi, long associated with BBC Urdu. He is read in both countries for his sharp, satirical, outspoken writing.
Modi hai to mumkin hai
"With Modi, anything is possible": a famous BJP slogan in the 2019 general election, presenting the Prime Minister as a leader who can pull off any difficult task.

h: Salute Neha Bora, but do not make her a messiah
dek: Gujarati columnist Urvish Kothari pairs his praise for the movement's brightest face with a warning: India's habit is to worship heroes, and that habit has long eaten away at movements.
body: AISA national president Neha Bora has become the most recognised face of the second phase of the Jantar Mantar movement. In the first phase came a 23-day fast, then daily clashes with the Delhi Police at the barricades, detentions and viral photographs. Urvish Kothari openly praises her courage, and then begins his real point from there.

He compares Neha with Irom Sharmila, whose identity was shaped by years of lonely fasting and the image of a tube in her nose. Neha's style is different: she comes across not as a victim but as an activist who steps forward to fight. The writer also notes that Left politics today survives mainly on campuses, and that like Kanhaiya Kumar, Neha faces the question of how far she can go beyond the campus under the CPI (ML) banner.

Here is the warning. Supporters are calling her a lioness and the Rani of Jhansi. Kothari says the praise is understandable, but unconditional praise sometimes does more harm than sharp criticism, because it stops you from seeing the details. Charisma produces fewer comrades and more devotees, and the remedy is to keep capable people from different fields around oneself.

The writer approves of one thing Neha did: when she was compared with CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, she spoke of unity, not rivalry. The danger lies less in the leader than in the public's appetite to divide every story into hero and villain.

Kothari recalls that a section of this same intellectual class once made a messiah of Narendra Modi too. The movement should not revolve around one person; it is also being carried forward by nameless people bearing police pressure and by independent journalists. What he wishes for are leaders who admit their flaws and change course, whether Neha, the CJP's leaders or Rahul Gandhi.
nazar: At the height of a movement, this cool-headed voice is needed. Faces give a movement strength, but they also make it easy for power to target, defame or buy off a face. The aim of the fight against Gyanesh Kumar is to restore an institution's credibility, and that will be done not on the strength of one lioness but on the strength of thousands of unnamed voters and activists.
sawal: Do we want leaders, or someone to fight on our behalf?
ref: Irom Sharmila
A Manipur activist who fasted for about sixteen years demanding the repeal of AFSPA (the Armed Forces Special Powers Act), during which she was force-fed through a nasal tube.
AISA
All India Students' Association, a Left student organisation linked to the CPI (ML) Liberation, with deep roots in JNU and campuses in Bihar and UP.

h: This is a crisis of trust, and the police cannot solve it
dek: Sanjib Kr Baruah argues that the SIR fight has moved from the courts to the street, and the government is trying to settle with barricades a question that only transparency can answer.
body: On the morning of 10 October, central Delhi looked like a cantonment. According to the writer, nearly 23,000 police and paramilitary personnel were deployed, and entry to and exit from Jantar Mantar was tightly controlled. The target is the Election Commission, the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter lists, and above all Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

Baruah lists three features of this movement. First, the debate has left petitions and Commission hearings behind and come to the street, and its centre has become one man. The order of demands is clear: first Gyanesh Kumar's resignation, then the rollback of SIR. He says the reason is that the Commission has no visible way to hear complaints, and reports have come out that many of its decisions were not taken by consensus.

Second, the crowd has no single leader but many: students, unemployed young people, Rahul and Priyanka Gandhi, YouTuber Dhruv Rathee and the CJP's Abhijeet Dipke. The writer sees this as a strength, because it cannot be dismissed as one party's sponsored show, and also a weakness, because the government has no single face to talk to.

The third and deepest point is the burden of proof. If a name is cut, who must prove it, the Commission or the voter? The government says SIR is removing dead, duplicate and illegal voters. Protesters ask why people who voted in 2024 are getting deletion notices in 2026. In the writer's words, this has turned an administrative exercise into an anxiety about citizenship.

So far the government's answer has been barricades, detentions and Section 163 of the BNSS. Baruah calls this the wrong diagnosis: this is a crisis of trust, not of law and order. He suggests inviting the Opposition, agreeing on a transparent and time-bound way of checking the lists, and placing it before a citizens' tribunal. The movement has come from Bengaluru to Delhi and may reach Mumbai and Patna, and he warns that how SIR is handled in October 2026 will shape how India votes in 2029.
nazar: Baruah's most useful question is about the burden of proof. If, in a democracy, voters have to run from office to office to prove they exist, the weight falls first on the poor, migrant workers, Dalits, Adivasis and minorities, who have the fewest papers. Twenty-three thousand personnel cannot answer that question.
A citizens' tribunal may sound mild, but it would be the government's real test: if the lists are clean, why fear an open inquiry?
sawal: Should the voter prove they are a voter, or the Commission?
ref: Section 163 of the BNSS
The section of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita that lets district authorities ban gatherings in an area. It replaces Section 144 of the old CrPC.
SIR
Special Intensive Revision: the Election Commission's fresh check of voter lists, in which voters were asked for documents and large numbers of names are alleged to have been cut.

h: Jantar Mantar 2.0: a former diplomat on democracy's slide
dek: Former diplomat Malay Mishra puts the Commission's make-up, SIR and a silent court side by side to show how a democracy is weakened with its own tools.
body: Abhijeet Dipke's Cockroach Janta Party announced a nationwide movement at Jantar Mantar from 10 October, which it calls Jantar Mantar 2.0. The main demand is the removal of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The CJP alleges that SIR took away the vote from 13.4 crore voters in 30 states and union territories, and that the process has no constitutional sanction. Its demands go further: dissolve the Commission in its present form, cancel elections held after SIR, and prosecute Gyanesh Kumar.

Malay Mishra's concern begins with how the Commission is built. According to him, the three-member committee that chooses commissioners was created by an amendment passed by voice vote without the Opposition taking part, and commissioners were given lifelong legal protection. Then it emerged that two commissioners recorded written dissent 14 times in ten months, yet later appeared at a press conference saying all decisions were unanimous.

The writer's second fear is about the use of Forms 6 and 7. He alleges that names were added, deleted and changed arbitrarily through the ECINET platform, perhaps targeting a particular community. He links this to the citizenship register, One Nation One Election and delimitation, an agenda that could divide the country into citizens and non-citizens.

He names unemployment, jobless growth, rising inequality and corporate capture of resources as the ground on which young people's anger has grown. His complaint against the Supreme Court is that it has not taken up so large a matter on its own.

Finally he cites Levitsky and Ziblatt's book How Democracies Die: elected leaders can hollow out democracy using democracy's own institutions. In his view, the crackdown on protests may be the government's last throw, and the world is watching India.
nazar: When a former diplomat writes in this language, it shows the unease is no longer limited to students and the Opposition; people who have been inside the system are also questioning the Commission's credibility. The 13.4 crore figure and the tampering through ECINET are still allegations, and only an open inquiry can give this debate solid ground.

The sharpest point is the court's silence. If the institution expected to protect the Constitution stays quiet even after the noise on the street, people begin to treat the street itself as the court.
sawal: If the court stays silent, who will plead for the Constitution?
ref: How Democracies Die
A 2018 book by Harvard political scientists Steven Levitsky and Daniel Ziblatt, arguing that democracies today die less by coups and more slowly at the hands of elected governments.
Forms 6 and 7
Applications to add a name to the voter list (Form 6) and to object to a name and have it removed (Form 7).

h: Gyanesh Kumar has brought a scattered opposition to one table
dek: Apoorva Mandhani argues that anger at the Election Commission has built a new alliance of MPs, student groups and civil society.
body: From the barricades of Delhi to Shivaji Park in Mumbai, protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar are spreading. Apoorva Mandhani says the question of names cut from voter lists and the SIR has brought together forces that used to fight separately. ThePrint has named the movement its 'Newsmaker of the Week'.

She lists the scenes of recent days: Rahul Gandhi climbing a barricade with the tricolour, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra pushed into a police van while holding the Constitution, AISA president Neha Bora lying on the road, opposition MPs sitting for hours under a tree near Akashvani Bhawan before being detained. In Mumbai, Uddhav and Raj Thackeray led a march carrying only the tricolour. Everyone has one demand: the CEC must resign and the SIR must be scrapped.

She links this to the NEET protests. Then too came a phase of fatigue and despair, with rumours that the education minister would not go, but in the end Dharmendra Pradhan had to resign. Her argument is that a movement that can remove a cabinet minister can also remove the CEC, and this time it is better organised.

According to the piece, Rahul Gandhi's image began to change with the Bharat Jodo Yatra, and this movement looks like the high point of that change. The 'vote chori' (vote theft) charge he has made since last year was sharpened by an Indian Express investigation. The opposition MPs' demands are now clearer and harder: resignation, scrapping the SIR, and a probe into the alleged manipulation of voter lists.

Students and civil society have become equal partners. Between 26 September and 4 October, people like Neha Bora, Yogendra Yadav, Prashant Bhushan, Anjali Bhardwaj and Dipankar Bhattacharya were detained again and again, on one day about 500 people. She sees growing trust among these groups. In Neha Bora's words this fight belongs to no single flag, and the contest is now between the opposition and citizens on one side, and the Commission and the BJP on the other.
nazar: The real news in this piece is the alliance. Movements in India have often fallen apart because parties treated students as a crowd and students saw parties as opportunists. If MPs, student groups and citizens' groups can now walk together without lowering each other's flags, that is a bigger challenge for the government than for the Commission.

But the lesson of NEET cuts both ways: a minister's resignation changes a face, not a system. If the demand shrinks to Gyanesh Kumar alone, the next commissioner will come out of the same structure. The test of this movement is whether it can carry its demand to the selection process and the transparency of voter lists.
sawal: Will one resignation restore trust, or must the whole structure change?
ref: NEET protests
Student protests over alleged irregularities in NEET, the medical entrance exam, with big demonstrations at Jantar Mantar in July; according to the piece, the education minister had to resign.
SIR
Special Intensive Revision: a house-to-house check of voter lists, accused of cutting crores of names, and the root of this movement.

h: A view from Lahore: the fight now moves to the streets, the courts and public opinion
dek: Pakistani columnist Aamir Khakwani argues that with no numbers in Parliament, the opposition's fight will now be fought on the streets, in court and in public opinion.
body: Aamir Khakwani is a well-known Lahore columnist, and his piece tries to explain to Pakistani readers why India is in such turmoil. He begins with the Indian Express report of 23 September, which said two members of the Election Commission, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had lodged written objections at least 14 times in ten months that key decisions were issued without their knowledge or approval.

The real blow, he says, falls on young voters. Form 6 now asks whether the applicant or their relatives were on the previous SIR roll; Khakwani says this hits the children of migrant workers and people with incomplete papers. He mentions Congress MP Dharamvir Gandhi's claim that about 13 crore names were cut, but this is an opposition allegation, not the finding of any inquiry.

The column also questions how the Chief Election Commissioner was appointed. The Supreme Court had put the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the Chief Justice on the selection panel; the government changed the law and replaced the Chief Justice with a Union minister, giving itself the majority. The writer recalls that the Commission had called Rahul Gandhi's Mahadevpura allegation baseless, and says the objections from inside the Commission now lend weight to that suspicion.

The Commission's reply that its decisions are unanimous seems weak to him: repeated written objections and a complaint that reached the Cabinet Secretary say otherwise. He also cites the Supreme Court notice of 5 October, which said decisions must be unanimous or by majority.

His conclusion is plain. The opposition lacks the special majority in Parliament needed to remove the Chief Election Commissioner, so the fight will be in the streets, the courts and public opinion. He recalls the Emergency and guesses that this youth movement could become a big challenge for the BJP by 2029.
nazar: The column offers little new reporting, but it puts the whole picture together from the outside, and that is its value. Today, as former chief ministers and student leaders are loaded into police buses on the same day in Delhi, Khakwani's point gets sharper: a fight shut out of Parliament comes to the street, and closing the street does not end the question of trust. Figures like 13 crore are still claims; the movement's strength lies in demanding they be proven, not in repeating them.
sawal: If the road through Parliament is shut, which door does democracy use?
ref: Aamir Khakwani
A senior Lahore journalist and Urdu columnist who writes regularly on politics and society.
CEC selection panel
Since the 2023 law the panel has the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and a Union minister; earlier the Supreme Court had placed the Chief Justice on it.

h: Dipankar Bhattacharya: when institutions fall silent, only the street is left
dek: The CPI(ML) general secretary argues that after the voter-list irregularities and the cracks inside the Election Commission, people have no option left but to protest.
body: Dipankar Bhattacharya begins his piece with 2 October. He sees the Gandhi Jayanti protests, from Kolkata to Delhi and Mumbai, as unprecedented in scale and calls the protesters heirs to Gandhi's non-violent tradition. He likens the government's response to the repression of colonial times, but also mentions the viral video in which protesters fan a police officer who had fainted.

The writer lists the movement's three demands: the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, scrapping the SIR, and restoring the rights of voters who were wrongly deleted. To these he adds the demand to repeal the 2023 law which, he says, tilted the selection of commissioners in the government's favour.

His biggest argument rests on the cracks inside the Commission. Citing Indian Express reports, he writes that two of the three commissioners recorded 14 objections in ten months, and that the heads of 11 appellate tribunals listed at least five defects in the appeals portal. Citing other reports, he also mentions lakhs of Form 7 appeals in West Bengal and 16.18 lakh names added in Uttar Pradesh without details.

The writer also cites a survey by his own party: comparing the rolls before and after the SIR at 50 booths in 10 Bihar seats, he says, 17 per cent of names were found wrongly deleted. He also speaks of more than 13 crore (130 million) people losing their vote, but this is his claim and the piece gives no source for it.

In the end he says that when the court has given the Commission a free hand and Parliament offers no way out, democracy comes to rest on the people's political sense. He sees hope for change in the 30 September INDIA bloc meeting and in the activism of students and Gen Z, and asks readers to keep their eyes on the streets.
nazar: This is a party leader's piece and several figures come from his own side, so they should be read as claims. Still, its strength is that it presents the movement not just as anger but as a list: which objection, from which tribunal, through which form. Today, as thousands are packed into buses in Delhi, the real challenge for the government is to answer this list, not to stop the crowd.
sawal: Who will answer the objections raised inside the Commission?
ref: Dipankar Bhattacharya
General secretary of the CPI(ML) Liberation; a well-known voice of the Left movement in Bihar and across India.
Form 7
The Election Commission form used to seek deletion of a name from the voter list or to object to it.

h: Brazil's election, in Washington's shadow
dek: With Flavio Bolsonaro ahead after the first round, journalist Maria Martha Bruno asks whether the 25 October verdict will be decided by Brazil's voters or by Trump's America.
body: In the first round of Brazil's presidential election, far-right senator Flavio Bolsonaro got 47 percent of the vote and sitting President Lula 45 percent. The second round is on 25 October, and a far-right majority in the new Congress is seen as certain. Bruno, who is associated with the Brazilian investigative outlet Agencia Publica, argues that this result is not just about domestic politics but also about American interference.

She lays out the sequence. In July 2025 Trump imposed tariffs of up to 50 percent on Brazil and demanded that the coup plot case against Jair Bolsonaro be dropped. Sanctions were placed on the judges hearing the case, reportedly after lobbying in Washington by Bolsonaro's son Eduardo. Brazil did not bend, and in September 2025 Jair was sentenced to 27 years.

In May 2026 Flavio, Eduardo and their associates met Trump at the White House. Two days later the US declared two of Brazil's big criminal gangs, Comando Vermelho and the PCC, terrorist organisations. According to Bruno, these gangs do not fall within the definition of terrorism in Brazilian law, but the label feeds the far right's story in which every different identity is a threat. Then came new tariffs of up to 37.5 percent, and a leaked document reportedly set conditions such as access to critical minerals and allowing Jair to stand for election, which Brazil rejected.

The most frightening part of the piece is the example of Venezuela. There too, a story of threat was first built by calling gangs terrorists, then boats at sea were attacked, and in January 2026 US forces entered Caracas and seized Maduro.

Lula has made this his issue: Brazil is nobody's backyard. Bruno warns that if Lula wins, a harsh US reaction and the false fraud claims of 2022 could come back to life. The real question before voters is sovereignty.
nazar: The piece says little about Lula's own weaknesses. The reasons for the first-round defeat, an ageing party, the lack of a successor, voters troubled by crime and rising prices, are just as real as the outside pressure. Still, the chain Bruno links together, tariffs, sanctions on judges, calling gangs terrorists, shows that interference in elections today comes not with tanks but with trade and labels.

For the Indian reader this is a mirror: when a superpower pressures another country's courts and markets for its favourite leader, democracy is protected not by the ballot box alone but by the backbone of institutions.
sawal: When tariffs start deciding votes, where is sovereignty left?
ref: Jair Bolsonaro
Former President of Brazil (2019-2022). After losing the 2022 election he was sentenced to 27 years in September 2025 in the coup plot case. His son Flavio is now a presidential candidate.
Second round (runoff)
In Brazil, if no candidate wins more than half of the valid votes in the first round, voting is held again between the top two. This time it is on 25 October.

h: Three years of Gaza: no peace without justice
dek: Marking three years since 7 October, a Dawn editorial says that even a ceasefire in name has not stopped the killing in Gaza, and that without justice for Palestine no peace in West Asia will last.
body: Marking three years since the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023, Pakistan's newspaper Dawn wrote that the people of Gaza are still living in a nightmare. Israel has tightened the siege further, and more than 1,400 people have been killed even during the so-called ceasefire in force since October 2025.

According to the editorial, more than 74,000 people have been killed in Gaza since October 2023, most of them civilians. Entire families have been wiped out, and experts believe the trauma will last for generations. Doctors Without Borders accuses Israel of suffocating Gaza and continuing a genocide.

The paper says the effects have spread across the region. Israel has occupied more land in Lebanon and Syria and attacked Iran and Yemen, with the US joining in some operations. In the West Bank, hardline Jewish settlers are running a campaign of terror against Palestinians. According to the editorial, Hamas has agreed to give up its weapons, but the peace process is stuck because Israel is not ready to end the occupation.

Dawn argues that Gaza was in misery even before 7 October, and that Hamas's action gave Israel an excuse for even harsher attacks. When people are stripped of basic rights, ancestral land and peace, they resist in every way they can.

In the end the editorial calls the two-state solution impossible, and calls the solutions proposed by forums such as the Board of Peace a cruel joke on the Palestinians. Its conclusion is simple: all occupied territories must be freed and the killing of civilians must be accounted for, otherwise talk of peace is meaningless.
nazar: Dawn's editorial is bitter and may also seem one-sided. The pain of the Israeli civilians and hostages killed on 7 October is almost absent from it, and words like genocide are still allegations under consideration in international courts. But the figures speak for themselves: 1,400 deaths in a year of ceasefire show that the war has not stopped; only its name has changed.

India, once among the loudest voices for Palestine, is almost silent on this question today. A neighbouring newspaper's reminder that there is no peace without justice is a question for our own foreign policy too.
sawal: If people die even in a ceasefire, whose ceasefire is it?
ref: 7 October 2023
The day Hamas attacked southern Israel, killing about 1,200 people and taking hundreds hostage. Israel then launched a war on Gaza.
Board of Peace

An international forum set up on a US initiative after the Gaza ceasefire, given the task of overseeing Gaza's administration and reconstruction. Many on the Palestinian side see it as an arrangement imposed without their say.

h: Beyond the mango basket: the real test of India-Bangladesh ties
dek: Analyst Faisal Mahmud says Haribhanga mangoes, hilsa and jamdani kept the door open between Dhaka and Delhi, but questions such as Hasina, river water and the border now demand direct political talks.
body: After the July 2024 uprising ended Sheikh Hasina's fifteen-year rule, Dhaka chose to avoid a head-on clash with Delhi. Its tools were Haribhanga mangoes, hilsa fish, jamdani and Tangail saris, cultural events and constant dialogue. Faisal Mahmud, managing editor of the Dhaka newspaper Daily Wada, believes this soft diplomacy kept relations from turning into lasting hostility, but that it has now reached its limit.

He gives the examples himself. In July 2025 Yunus's interim government sent Prime Minister Modi a thousand kilos of mangoes. It was a gesture of sweetness in the relationship, but the problems stayed where they were. Hasina is in India and Dhaka wants her extradited. Disputes continue over the border, transit and the treatment of Bangladeshi citizens. After Tarique Rahman's BNP government came in in February 2026, visa services were restored, but numbers have not returned to pre-2024 levels.

Bangladesh's High Commission in Delhi held a jamdani exhibition, and in April 2026 three hundred saris by weavers from Tangail and Pabna sold out in twenty-four hours. But Dhaka's mistake was to take access for influence. Admiring Bengali craft does not mean agreeing with Dhaka's strategy, and the Tangail sari itself got tangled in a geographical indication (GI) dispute.
India invited Tarique Rahman for a bilateral visit and to the BRICS summit, but he did not go. Dhaka says a summit needs the right atmosphere and mutual respect. Such a visit needs a concrete agenda.

His conclusion is that the old relationship rested on security cooperation, electricity and the political arrangements of the Hasina era, which have now fallen apart. Trade deals, water sharing, the border and intelligence cooperation will not be settled at the dinner table. The mangoes kept the door open; now the real bargaining has to happen on the other side of it.
nazar: This piece is written from Dhaka's point of view, but its lesson is for Delhi too. In the Hasina era India bet on a single party and made the relationship rest on individuals. Now that Bangladesh has a newly elected government, Delhi too must go beyond gifts and statements and talk honestly about questions such as the Teesta, killings at the border and the treatment of Bangla speakers in Bengal and Assam.
Mahmud's most useful line is that access is not influence. Ties with a neighbour begin in the heart, but they last on trust.
sawal: The mango opened the door, but who will walk in?
ref: Haribhanga mango
A famous mango variety from the Rangpur region of Bangladesh. Governments in Dhaka have for years sent it as a gift to leaders of India and other countries.
Teesta water dispute
An old quarrel between India and Bangladesh over sharing the waters of the Teesta river. In 2011 an agreement was almost settled, but it stalled over the West Bengal government's opposition.

h: Government and opposition: the old illness of Bangladesh's new parliament
dek: Daily Star editor Mahfuz Anam takes stock from 1991 to today and says Bangladesh has never given the opposition its due, and that the same mistakes are being repeated even on the clean slate after the July uprising.
body: Mahfuz Anam begins with the February 1991 election, which the BNP won, leaving the Awami League, which had taken its victory for granted, stunned. Khaleda Zia went against her own party's manifesto, accepted the opposition's demand and returned the country to a parliamentary system. According to Anam, this could have become the foundation of cooperation between government and opposition.

That did not happen. Sheikh Hasina called that election subtly rigged, and the opposition chose to paralyse parliament to show the government as a failure. Anam tells a story: when the parliament bell rang, Hasina announced a walkout, and when asked why, said do what you like. Then came a period of boycotts, resignations, week-long strikes and street violence that destroyed parliament's standing.

The irony was that under a caretaker government the opposition won every time: the Awami League in 1996, the BNP in 2001, the Awami League again in 2008. This cemented the belief that the politics of obstruction pays. In 2011 the Awami League ended the caretaker system, and Anam describes the elections of 2014, 2018 and 2024 as wholly manipulated, which turned the police, bureaucracy, courts and even universities partisan.

The July uprising offered a clean slate, but the new parliament got off to a bad start. The BNP refused a separate oath for the constitutional reform council, and let 16 of 133 ordinances, those dealing with judicial independence, enforced disappearances, the Anti-Corruption Commission and the Human Rights Commission, lapse without consulting the opposition. Of 50 standing committees, only the chair of the Public Accounts Committee went to the opposition.

Anam holds up a mirror to both sides. The ruling BNP should listen more, and the opposition, many of whose complaints are fair, should avoid threats to take to the streets, because destabilising a government after a widely accepted election does not serve democracy.
nazar: This is the almost autobiographical testimony of an editor who has watched thirty-five years of mistakes up close. Its most valuable part is the recognition that in South Asia the opposition is treated not as an alternative government in waiting but as an enemy, and the failure to agree even on laws such as those against enforced disappearance is proof of it.

But the advice to the opposition to stay off the streets seems a little hasty. In a country where parliament has been made meaningless again and again, the street too has been part of democracy. For the Indian reader this question is not unfamiliar: committees, debate in the House and respect for the opposition are the real test of parliamentary democracy.
sawal: Is the opposition an enemy, or an alternative government?
ref: Caretaker government system

An arrangement in force in Bangladesh from 1996 to 2011, in which a neutral interim government took charge before elections. In 2011 the Awami League government abolished it through a constitutional amendment.
July Charter
A shared document of reforms agreed among political parties after the 2024 student and people's uprising, with promises of changes to the constitution, elections and institutions.

h: Punjab's missing daughters
dek: A Dawn editorial says that for the police, hundreds of cases of missing girls in Pakistan's Punjab are merely stories of elopement, when sex trafficking gangs are behind many of them.
body: During the hearing of a missing person case in the Lahore High Court, the police chief of Pakistan's Punjab admitted that more than 500 cases of missing girls in the province remain unresolved. The court expressed shock at the figure, spoke of the families' pain and pointed to police negligence. When Chief Justice Aalia Neelum asked what mechanism existed for cases involving women and children, the answer was that special committees would be formed.

Dawn's editorial calls this a matter of shame. According to it, girls who return are suspected of sexual abuse by their own relatives and have to bear the stigma of dishonour. Many girls are sold to sex trafficking gangs, and there are also cases in which a girl who fled a forced marriage is recorded as abducted.

Most of the girls come from poor families and areas, so the police close the case without investigation, calling it an elopement. The paper asks: if a court order is needed to investigate an abduction, what is this if not indifference and a lack of accountability?

The figures are frightening. In 2022 police data, 3,571 abducted girls and women were missing in Punjab, and between 2017 and January 2022, 40,585 cases of abduction of women were registered in the province.

The editorial demands institutional reform, the criminalisation of patriarchal customs that keep women confined, and that every case of a girl missing for a long time be investigated as possible trafficking rather than treated as a domestic quarrel.
nazar: On this side of the border the story is not unfamiliar. In India too thousands of girls go missing every year, and police stations echo with the same line: she must have run off with someone. A poor parent's complaint stays a piece of paper until a court scolds.

Dawn's most important argument is that the idea of honour itself becomes the girl's enemy: even when she returns, she is treated as the guilty one. Until society sees a missing daughter not as a shame but as the victim of a crime, police indifference will keep getting the cover of society's silence.
sawal: Whose convenience is it to call a missing daughter a runaway?
ref: Lahore High Court
The highest court of Pakistan's Punjab. Its Chief Justice, Aalia Neelum, is the first woman to hold the post.
Human trafficking
Taking a person for exploitation through deceit, force or sale, for example for the sex trade, bonded labour or forced marriage.

h: Irked by 'Sharad Utsav': Bengal copies America's culture war
dek: Shoaib Daniyal argues that Hindutva's objection to an old Bengali name for Durga Puja comes not from Bengal's soil but from America's 'War on Christmas'.
body: West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari told the Assembly that puja committees which call Durga Puja 'Sharad Utsav' (autumn festival) should not get permission for stalls, because communists treat Sanatan Dharma as mere culture. A few days later Sanjeev Sanyal, a member of the Prime Minister's Economic Advisory Council, called the term an attempt to slowly secularise the festival, in which the goddess is left as just a backdrop for selfies.

Shoaib Daniyal sees this as part of a larger Hindutva anxiety: an anxiety to strip festivals of everything other than religion. After appeals to limit the themes of pandals (festival marquees), idol orders in Kolkata have fallen. The Vishwa Hindu Parishad asked for a ban on meat around pandals, and Hindutva groups attacked a restaurant whose billboard showed gods and goddesses eating mutton biryani.

Daniyal accepts that every big mass festival is a mix of religion and culture, and that conservative religious movements opposing this is understandable. But the argument over the word is strange. In Bengali, Sharad Utsav is simply a slightly formal name for Durga Puja, far older than communism in India. The CPI(M) pointed to Tagore's 1908 play Sharadotsav, and Adhikari himself used the same word in his greetings in 2022.

According to the writer, this quarrel has been imported from America. Since the 2000s, conservatives there such as Bill O'Reilly have raised a din about a 'War on Christmas', because some people had started saying 'Season's Greetings' instead of 'Merry Christmas'. There was no war, but the political gain was big, and later Trump himself became the leader of this fight.

Hindutva social media handles often borrow the language of white nationalists, and calling opponents agents of George Soros is part of the same import. The irony is that the Western right that Hindutva holds up as its ideal is seeing growing racism against Indians and Hinduism.
nazar: In Bengal, Durga Puja has never been only a ritual. It is a shared festival in which artisans, dhakis (drummers), shopkeepers and people of every faith find their livelihood and their joy. When themes, food and even the name start being decided from above, the first blow falls on their bread, as the falling idol orders show.

The second point goes deeper. A movement that calls itself the guardian of native identity is borrowing its battles from America's culture war, and reading Tagore's language through foreign glasses. Bengal's culture needs no one's certificate.
sawal: Who will name the festival, the people or those in power?
ref: Sharadotsav
Rabindranath Tagore's 1908 play about the autumn festival. In Bengali, Sharad Utsav is a familiar, somewhat formal word for Durga Puja.
War on Christmas
A campaign by the American right since the 2000s that paints inclusive phrases like 'Happy Holidays' as an attack on Christianity.

h: Detained before the march to Delhi: CJP activists picked up in Bengal
dek: A day before the 10 October protest at Jantar Mantar, police in several districts of Bengal shuttled Cockroach Janta Party activists between homes, hotels and police stations; the police deny allegations of beatings.
body: Ahead of the protest in Delhi on 10 October demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, police in West Bengal picked up several activists of the Cockroach Janta Party, the CJP. According to Alt News, this happened across the state on 8 October.

The most talked-about case is that of Sheikh Abdul Hafiz. He had come to Kolkata with four companions, Amina Khan, Sana Rahman, Sananda Ghosh and Habibul Islam, to catch a train to Delhi. The CJP alleges that at around 8.30 in the morning the police entered their hotel room in New Town without giving a reason and without a warrant, shoved the women and snatched their phones. The police say everyone was released at 6.30 in the evening, but the party could not trace them until 9.30 at night, when Hafiz posted videos on Instagram.

In these videos Hafiz alleged beatings, abuse, and being forced to record a statement that the police had not mistreated them. He says they were also threatened with harsh charges and years in jail if they kept protesting. The officer in charge of Bidhannagar North police station admitted that the activists had been brought in at the request of the Eco Park police, but denied any beating at his station.

In Howrah three activists were picked up from their homes in the afternoon and released around midnight after being moved through several police stations. Reports of police action also came from Malda, East and West Medinipur and Sonarpur. The party alleges that families were pressured too: in Sonarpur a student's father was called to the police station and told to stop his son.
Hafiz is the same young man who was attacked in his village in Bankura after returning from Jantar Mantar in August. His father, Sheikh Mohammad Mafiq, who came to save him, died on 15 August.
nazar: Stopping a citizen before they can even go to the capital to protest is not an arrangement for law and order but for fear. And when the target is a young man who lost his father because of this very movement, the question grows heavier.
The allegations are still allegations, and the police deny them. But the simplest way to investigate is to put the police station records and camera footage on the table.
sawal: Whom does an arrest before a protest protect?
ref: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)
An organisation of students and young people that campaigned this year against the NEET irregularities and is now protesting to demand the Chief Election Commissioner's resignation.
Preventive detention
Police detaining someone in the name of stopping a crime before it happens. Courts have said again and again that its use should be the exception, not the rule.

h: Twelve hours at Surat's looms, a fight for eight
dek: Workers in Surat's embroidery and textile units have for two months been demanding an eight-hour day and a weekly day off, which the law already provides.
body: In April 2020 a video from Surat's Udhna railway station became the symbol of the helplessness of migrant workers stranded in the lockdown. More than six years later Surat is again in the news because of its workers, this time because of a movement. Newslaundry's report tells the story of this movement.

Surat is among the country's big textile and embroidery hubs. Workers here are demanding three things: an eight-hour working day, one paid day off a week, and compliance with labour laws. The unions say these are not new demands but rights the law has already granted. Yet many workers are still made to work twelve-hour shifts.

The movement began on 16 August in the embroidery units of the Amroli area and slowly spread to other industrial areas of the city. The labour department held several rounds of meetings with the unions and industry representatives, but the dispute was not resolved. Industry argues that if the demands are fully accepted, costs will rise and business will suffer.

In the last week of September, Surat's deputy labour commissioner directed industry bodies to comply with the new labour codes. The unions say no big difference is visible on the ground. Meanwhile tension also rose in Amroli. Over allegations of stone pelting and forcing factories to shut, the police registered three FIRs, arrested eight people, and cases were filed against about 500 people.
The movement is now almost two months old. For the workers it is no longer just about hours or days off; it has become a question of a life with dignity and better working conditions.
nazar: When workers have to take to the streets even for a right written into law, and the response is cases against five hundred people, it tells you whom the law serves on paper and whom on the ground. In the era of the new labour codes, Surat is a test of whether the government can make employers comply.
sawal: Since when did asking for a right written in law become a crime?
ref: Eight-hour working day
A victory of labour movements around the world more than a hundred years old, which found a place in India's factory laws even before independence.
Udhna station, 2020
The Surat station where, during the Covid lockdown, crowds of migrant workers desperate to go home and their helplessness were caught on camera.

h: Kutch port workers finally get ESI, but where are the hospitals?
dek: Kutch district, home to ports such as Kandla and Mundra, was brought under Employees' State Insurance from 1 October, but the health care set-up is still on paper.
body: Gujarat's Kutch district is a major centre of ports, mines, salt, chemicals, steel and cement, but its workers had so far been outside Employees' State Insurance, or ESI. After a Union Labour Ministry notification of 25 September, 15 such districts of Gujarat including Kutch, and 16 partly covered districts, came under the scheme from 1 October.

This decision did not come on its own. The ESI Adhikar Manch, a coalition of trade unions, social organisations and lawyers, had written to the government in October 2023. Then the Shri Kutch General Mazdoor Sangh filed a public interest petition in the Gujarat High Court. It said the district has 944 registered factories and 43 hazardous industries. In November 2025 the court sought affidavits from the government, and on 29 September it disposed of the petition with liberty to return if grievances remained.

The ESIC survey figures in the affidavits are important. In Gandhidham, of 13,675 employees in the surveyed establishments, 10,300 earn less than 21,000 rupees. In Mundra 9,580 of 16,943 fall in this bracket, and at Adani Ports and SEZ 4,898 of 10,575 employees. Dispensaries, branch offices and tie-ups with hospitals are proposed in Bhuj, Mundra and Gandhidham.

The problem is that contributions began to be deducted from 1 October, while the treatment facilities have not yet been built. By the estimate of a Gujarati newspaper, about nine crore rupees a month will be collected from Kutch, and an industry association too has asked where the service is in return.

The writer demands that ESIC make public a map and timeline for dispensaries and hospitals, empanel existing hospitals in the meantime, provide information in Gujarati and in the languages of migrant workers, and give workers a share in oversight.
nazar: That workers at one of the country's biggest private ports worked for years without social security says in itself where the worker stands in this model of development. Now that the right has come, it must not be allowed to become just a deduction from wages. Contract workers and those from other states are the first to be left out, and keeping an eye on them matters most.
sawal: The money is being deducted, but when will the treatment come?
