ref: Employees' State Insurance (ESI)

A social security scheme for workers in which both employer and employee contribute, and in return get medical care, sick leave and compensation for accidents. At present those earning up to 21,000 rupees are covered.
Code on Social Security, 2020
One of the four new labour codes, which brings ESI, the provident fund and other schemes together.

h: After eight years, signs of a student union election at AMU
dek: After a student's 19-day hunger strike and a blockade of the gates, Aligarh Muslim University has appointed election officers for student union polls.
body: At Aligarh Muslim University on 9 October, students' anger turned into celebration. The registrar issued two notifications: Professor Javed Talib of the law department was made chief election officer for the AMU student union election, and Professor Nazia Hasan for the Women's College students' union. Students say this is the answer to a demand ignored for eight years.

The movement began with a very small matter. There were repeated complaints of insects in the food at the Women's College mess, nothing changed, and the students allege they were mistreated when they protested. The protest, which started with the students of Abdullah Hall, slowly turned into a demand to restore the student union.

On 21 September Yasir Fahad, an MA student in Urdu, began an indefinite hunger strike. Students submitted a memorandum demanding elections within 48 hours; Fahad was suspended without a show-cause notice, and then all four gates of the campus were shut. On 7 October there were also allegations of heavy police deployment on campus. Students recall that last year too the Vice Chancellor had promised a date that was forgotten as soon as the crowd thinned.

The AMU student union's roots go back to the debating clubs of the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College, and its life membership was once given even to Mahatma Gandhi. The last election was held in 2018-19, whereas the Lyngdoh Committee guidelines call for an election every year.

Students say that without a union there is no one to raise issues such as being barred from exams in the name of attendance. Students at the Women's College hope that once a union is formed, the way to their own representation will open too, though the report also notes that a movement started by women once again ended up with a man as its face.
nazar: For eight years the country's oldest Muslim educational institution had no elected voice of students. This is not just administrative negligence but a habit of keeping campus politics silent. Appointing election officers is the first step; a date and a fair election will be the real test. And it remains to be seen how much space the new union will give the women students who began this fight over mess food.
sawal: Who is afraid of an elected voice on campus?
ref: Lyngdoh Committee

A committee set up at the Supreme Court's direction whose recommendations have, since 2006, set the rules for student union elections in colleges and universities, such as annual elections and spending limits.
AMU's minority status
In 1967 the Supreme Court denied it; in 2024 the court overturned that ruling, but left the final decision to a bench of three judges.
photo_note: Sir Syed South Hall, Aligarh Muslim University

h: Wayanad is losing its cool, and coffee flowered in September
dek: Data from weather instruments set up in villages shows that this September Wayanad was about two degrees warmer than the average of the past three years, and the effect on farming is starting to show.
body: Wayanad, a hill district of Kerala, has long been known for its cool climate. A Down To Earth report says this identity is now wavering. Since the floods and landslides of 2018 and 2019, the Hume Centre for Ecology and Wildlife Biology in Kalpetta has run a community weather monitoring network across the district, which since 2024 has been collecting rainfall data from more than 200 places.

According to this network, the average temperature between 1 and 17 September 2026 was 29.2 degrees, while the average for the same period over the past three years was 27.2 to 27.3 degrees. From 11 to 17 September the mercury stayed above 30 degrees for seven days in a row. Bare soil temperature reached 39 degrees and it rained only four times.

The centre's director, C.K. Vishnudas, has warned that groundwater could fall fast, putting paddy and other crops in trouble. Coffee, pepper and arecanut farming depend on a set pattern of rainy and dry days, which can no longer be relied on. In September flowers were seen on a coffee plant, whereas flowering usually comes between December and February. The centre itself accepts that one example does not prove a trend.

Studies cited in the report say that with two degrees of global warming, robusta coffee yields in Wayanad could fall by about 12 percent on average. The rain behind the 2024 Mundakkai-Chooralmala landslide was estimated to have been about 10.8 percent heavier because of human-caused warming.

Satellite images show concrete construction growing and paddy fields shrinking. The report also cautiously says that a month of heat in an El Nino year does not prove a lasting change, but that the district is becoming less predictable.
nazar: This Wayanad report also matters because its data came not from some distant office but from instruments in villages. The biggest climate shocks fall on small farmers, Adivasi (indigenous) families and plantation workers, and having their own data can become a weapon in their fight.
sawal: If the hills lose their cool, where will the people of the hills go?
ref: El Nino
The unusual warming of Pacific Ocean waters, which in India often brings a weak monsoon and more heat.
Mundakkai-Chooralmala landslide
A landslide in Wayanad in July 2024 after heavy rain, in which hundreds of people died and several villages were destroyed.

h: After complaints from 11 students, JNU sacks MP professor
dek: After an inquiry by JNU's internal committee, Angomcha Bimol Akoijam, a professor and Congress MP from Manipur, has been dismissed over sexual harassment allegations; he denies them.
body: Jawaharlal Nehru University on Friday dismissed Professor Angomcha Bimol Akoijam with immediate effect. Akoijam teaches at the Centre for the Study of Social Systems and is also a Congress Lok Sabha MP from Manipur. Scroll reported the news citing a news agency and other newspapers.

According to the university, 11 students had accused him of sexual harassment. The complaints reached the internal committee about four months ago. The committee investigated, and the dismissal was decided on the basis of its findings. The committee's detailed report has not been made public.

The complaints allege that the professor, who lives on campus, used to invite students to gatherings at his home and make sexual advances there. Some complainants said vulgar remarks were made during classes and viva exams, and some even alleged that sex was demanded in exchange for marks.
Akoijam has denied all the allegations. He described the complainants as hatching a racist conspiracy and said his reputation was being damaged by unverified claims and lies.

The case also stands out because the accused is a sitting MP, and complaints against such powerful people usually hang for years. Here the journey from complaint to decision was completed in about four months, which is worth noting in itself. What shape the legal fight ahead will take is not yet clear.
nazar: Complaints of sexual harassment on campus are often buried under fear, the gap in power and long processes. Here, eleven people speaking up together and the committee reaching a finding in four months is worth noting. The accused must get every legal avenue to make his case.

But it would be wrong to see this decision through the lens of any party's win or loss. The question is whether internal committees at other institutions show the same seriousness, whatever the party or position of the accused.
sawal: Is every campus complaints committee this serious?
ref: Internal Complaints Committee
A committee every institution must set up under the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention) Act, 2013, to investigate such complaints.

h: Pakistan's prisons at 160 percent, three quarters of prisoners awaiting trial
dek: A new report by the Human Rights Commission and Justice Project Pakistan shows 1,10,513 people held in the country's prisons, which have room for about 69,000.
body: Pakistan's National Commission for Human Rights and Justice Project Pakistan released the Annual Prison Data Report 2026 in Islamabad. Based on official figures from prisons across the country, this is the second edition of the report, and Dawn has published its main findings.

According to the report, 1,10,513 people are held in Pakistan's prisons, against a sanctioned capacity of about 68,832. That means prisons are more than 160 percent full and more than 41,000 people are crammed in beyond capacity. Of them, 82,988 people, three out of four, are those whose trials are still going on. The number of undertrial prisoners alone is 14,000 more than the total capacity.

More than 28,000 people are in prison under the narcotics law, over a quarter of all prisoners, and their number has risen 43 percent since 2023. Compared with 2024, the number of women in prison has risen by about 46 percent, and more than 86 percent of children in prison are awaiting a verdict. The number of people on death row has fallen to 3,220.

Overcrowding is worst in the prisons of Punjab and Sindh. In Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan the number of prisoners has fallen and prisons are within capacity, which the report credits to probation, parole and other alternatives to prison.

Commission chairperson Rabiya Javeri Agha called this a crisis not just of overcrowding but of the whole criminal justice system, including long detention, delays in trials and obstacles to bail. The report recommends reform of the rules on bail and sureties, reducing unnecessary detention and strengthening oversight of prisons.
nazar: These figures are from across the border, but the picture is familiar. In India's prisons too a large share are undertrial prisoners, and among them the poor, Dalits, Adivasis and Muslims are over-represented. In both countries punishment begins even before the verdict.
Two of Pakistan's provinces have shown that parole and probation can reduce the burden on prisons. That lesson is useful for all of South Asia.
sawal: How can imprisonment before a verdict be called justice?
ref: Undertrial prisoners
People who are facing trial and have not yet been convicted by a court, but are in jail because they did not get bail or could not take it.
Justice Project Pakistan
A Lahore legal aid organisation that fights the cases of death row prisoners and prisoners from vulnerable groups.

h: Water falls, migration rises: Panna's Adivasi villages are emptying
dek: In Ranipur and Kalyanpur in Madhya Pradesh's Panna district, a changing climate has made farming a losing deal, and Adivasi (indigenous) families are leaving for wage work in Gujarat.
body: Adivasi families in the villages of Ranipur and Kalyanpur in Madhya Pradesh's Panna district once lived off farming and the forest. A ground report by The Mooknayak shows that a changing monsoon, rising heat and falling groundwater are now pushing them towards migration. According to Basant Lal Adivasi of Ranipur, twenty years ago the forest was three times what it is today; back then three or four percent of the village went out to earn, now about 65 percent do.

The life of 27-year-old Sangeeta Adivasi of Kalyanpur is a picture of this change. When one and a half acres could not run the household, her husband Lakhan went to work in a factory in Gujarat. For two years Sangeeta too has been going to Gujarat with her one-and-a-half-year-old daughter, and at the time of the report she was eight months pregnant. Her two older daughters live with their grandmother Harinbai, who goes out at night to fetch water.

Experts say the same. According to environmentalist Dr Indrabhan Singh Bundela, mahua, chaar and tendu leaves have declined over two decades, forest fires have increased, and several canals have not worked properly for ten to fifteen years. Dr P.N. Tripathi of the Krishi Vigyan Kendra says that in about five years the area under urad fell from one lakh (100,000) hectares to 45,000 hectares, because the rain now comes when the crop is ripening.

The government lists figures for tap-water schemes, farm ponds and recharge structures. Of the district's 10,039 handpumps, 384 are shut, 222 of them because the water level fell. But Madhav Singh's 30-foot well in Kalyanpur held 20-22 feet of water twenty years ago; now it holds 8-10 feet. According to former sarpanch (village head) Ramsajeevan Yadav, only two of the five handpumps work regularly.
Hope comes from Gandhigram, where 70-80 Adivasi families cleared the silt from two dried-up ponds with their own labour in March and April.
nazar: The debate on the climate crisis is often confined to urban heat and big conferences. This report from Panna reminds us that the heaviest price is being paid by Adivasis who have the least hand in this crisis, and whose children are growing up waiting for their parents at festival time.

The way official figures clash with village experience makes it clear that counting schemes is not enough. Adivasi rights over the forest, ample work under MGNREGA, and water management in the village's own hands: only these can slow the pace of migration.
sawal: When the well runs dry, where does the village go?
ref: Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK)
District-level government farm centres that advise farmers on new techniques, seeds and crops suited to the weather.
Distress migration
When people leave to work in other states or cities not for better opportunities, but because they can no longer make ends meet in the village.

h: No rain in Banni, Maldharis sell cattle for fodder
dek: Herders from Abdasa and Lakhpat in Kutch reached the dry Banni grassland, but found neither green grass nor government help.
body: The Banni grassland in Gujarat's Kutch usually turns into a lush, marshy area by mid-September. Relying on this, Maldhari herders of Abdasa and Lakhpat talukas bring their cattle here every year. This time, in an El Nino year, the July rains never came, and in the months before that the mercury had reached nearly 50 degrees. The Chhari Dhandh wetland, declared a Ramsar site ten months ago, also lies dry; not even birds can be seen.

Siddiq Bhai Jat, 65, of Ravrasar village, came in August with about 70 people after walking for seven days. Just carrying the women, children and buffaloes in vehicles cost him 60,000 rupees. Of his more than a hundred Kankrej cows, only 15-20 are giving milk. On top of that, a foreign thorny shrub called gando baval (mesquite) has spread across Banni, which cattle do not eat.

Green fodder is selling at 15 rupees a kilo, and each animal needs ten kilos a day. A cow's milk has fallen from eight to ten litres to one or two litres. Abdul Bhai Mutva of Mithdi village has seen his monthly earnings fall from 60,000-70,000 to 15,000. Haider Jat, 22, sold two buffaloes worth four lakh for one lakh.

In July and August herders from several communities went to the tehsildar's office and demanded that drought be declared. According to the report, they got sympathy, not help. Lakhpat has been declared drought-hit seven times in twenty years, yet there is no lasting arrangement.

The heaviest burden of migration falls on children and women. Children are missing school, women carry water over long distances in the heat, and the settlements have no toilets. In September some parts of Banni got rain, but Lakhpat and Abdasa are still dry and Kutch still has a heavy rainfall deficit. Many families do not even have the fare to take their cattle back.
nazar: Nomadic herders like the Maldharis stand in the front line of the climate crisis, but our relief policies are made for land and crops, not for moving herds. Drought is declared late and fodder aid is limited to a counted number of animals.
Protecting grazing lands from foreign shrubs, separate drought relief for herders and a fair price for milk: these three things can no longer be put off.
sawal: For those whose home is a moving herd, who will decide their relief?
ref: Maldhari
Traditional herding communities of Gujarat, especially Kutch and Saurashtra, who migrate seasonally in search of fodder and water.
Banni grassland
One of Asia's large grasslands, spread across Kutch, which turns marshy in the rains and is considered the home of the Kankrej cow and the Banni buffalo.

h: Vadhavan port: the sea will be taken, what of those who fish by hand?
dek: Compensation for the Vadhavan port being built in the Dahanu area of Palghar counted boat owners, but left out the women who fish without boats.
body: In Dahanu creek near Varor village in Maharashtra's Palghar district, as soon as the tide goes out, 60-year-old Amita Tandel steps down onto the wet shore. She has no boat; she catches fish and crabs by hand. She learnt to read the tides from her father and is raising her only son on this work alone. Now in these very waters the country's 13th major port, Vadhavan, is being built.

The project is a partnership of the Jawaharlal Nehru Port Authority and the Maharashtra Maritime Board. It includes a container terminal on an artificial island at sea, the reclamation of about 1,448 hectares of sea, and a breakwater more than ten kilometres long. The cost is estimated at over 76,000 crore rupees, and the government claims it will create more than ten lakh jobs. Road and rail corridors will pass through 16 villages.

The environmental impact assessment itself accepts that more than twenty thousand fishers depend on this area and that their access will shrink. Yet cash compensation and temporary income support have been kept only for boat owners, their workers and those who labour on boats. Hand fishers like Amita are not on this list. The government suggests training in cage fish farming as an alternative, which even young fishers do not trust.

The opposition is not new. In the nineties fishers went to the Supreme Court, after which the Dahanu Taluka Environment Protection Authority that was set up refused permission for the port in 1998. According to Narayan Patil, president of the struggle committee, the authority's members were changed in 2023, and later the same body gave the green signal. In February 2024 environmental clearance also came from the Centre.

A report by a government marine institute also accepts that reclamation and dredging will certainly damage fish breeding areas. Now reclamation and road work have begun, and prohibitory orders have been imposed around construction sites to stop protests. The fishers' question is simple: land can be compensated, but how will the sea be?
nazar: In the accounting of development, the people who often go missing are those whose work has no paperwork. Women who fish by hand neither own boats nor appear in any register, so they are left off the compensation list too.
The changed stance of the very authority that once said no to the port, and the ban on protest, both show that decisions are being taken not by sitting with the community but over its head.
sawal: Who will recognise the right to the sea of someone who has no papers?
ref: Intertidal zone
The part of the coast that is exposed at low tide and submerged at high tide. Crabs, shellfish and small fish live here.
Dahanu Taluka Environment Protection Authority
A body set up in 1996 on the Supreme Court's order, whose job was to protect Dahanu's fragile coastal and green area from big industry.

h: Choodu: memories of the forest in the ears of Paniya women
dek: Paniya women of the Nilgiris have long made ear ornaments from wax, leaves and red seeds, but as the forest shrinks, this craft is fading too.
by: Devaki B. Nair and Manikandan R.
body: In the settlements around Gudalur in Tamil Nadu's Nilgiris district, older women of the Ippimala Makkal, the Paniya community, wear a distinctive round ornament in their ears called the choodu. This report is part of PARI's project on endangered languages. The Paniya language is considered endangered, and in Tamil Nadu the community is on the list of Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups.

These families have their roots in neighbouring Wayanad. Generations ago they were brought here to labour in paddy fields and tea gardens. When bonded labour was abolished in 1976, some got land, but most still live on daily wages. When the nearby Mudumalai Tiger Reserve was created in 2008, many Adivasi (indigenous) families were uprooted and the forest was closed to them.

Making a choodu takes patience. Wax is taken from the hives of stingless bees without disturbing them. Kaida leaves, like screw pine, are passed through hot ash, dried, trimmed and rolled, and their white strip is wound onto a disc of wax. Then red rosary pea seeds are pressed into the soft wax in a circle. The earlobe is slowly stretched from childhood so the ornament can sit in it.

These materials are now hard to find. The kaida bushes along the rivers have been cleared, marshes have turned into tea, coffee and banana plantations, and stingless bee hives have grown scarce. Many women buy the seeds from hawkers and some make do with plastic strips. Finding kaida now takes half a day.

Women of the younger generation prefer hook earrings; people stare at anyone wearing a choodu alone. Still, older women make it for rituals, and old choodus are kept in a bamboo basket in the ancestors' corner of the house. They say that even if the ornament is given up, the identity of being Paniya is not.
nazar: This is not just the story of an ornament. When forests become plantations and Adivasis are evicted from their own land, their language, skills and everyday knowledge are wiped out along with them, and these cannot be rebuilt in any museum.
Policies that close forests in the name of conservation should also count which communities they have robbed of their cultural life.
sawal: When a forest is cut down, which memories are cut with it?
ref: Paniya (Ippimala Makkal)
An Adivasi community living in Kerala's Wayanad and Tamil Nadu's Nilgiris, whose history is tied to bonded farm labour. Their Dravidian language, Paniya, is considered endangered.
Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTG)
Those Adivasi communities the government considers most marginalised, for example because of declining population, low literacy and dependence on old livelihoods.

h: Women toil at the brick kiln, the register carries the men's names
dek: At the kilns of Gandhinagar, families from Chhattisgarh and Uttar Pradesh are bound by advance loans, and the women's labour is accounted for nowhere.
body: Around Adalaj and Uvarsad in Gujarat's Gandhinagar district there are dozens of chimney brick kilns. From late October to April raw bricks are moulded here, and they are fired until June. At each kiln forty or more jodis, that is husband-and-wife pairs, work 12 to 14 hours a day. Most workers come from Janjgir-Champa in Chhattisgarh and from Uttar Pradesh.

Rajni Kurre, 28, has been moulding bricks since she was twelve. Late last year she came here with her husband Rajesh and four children. Before the season an advance is taken from the contractor, and until it is paid off the family stays bound to the kiln. They get two to two and a half thousand rupees a week for expenses, which Rajni sees not as wages but as a loan. At the end of the season the contractor settles accounts after deducting the advance and expenses, and it is all done by word of mouth.

With no written record, workers never know how much they earned and how much debt remains. The Kurre family's old debt began with an advance taken for a relative's treatment. Illness, weddings, household expenses and the lack of work in the village all push people into this cycle.

Women knead clay and mould bricks just like men, but the kiln register carries the men's names and the money goes to them too. There is no place to bathe or wash and no toilets, there is no rest even during menstruation, and the care of children is also their job alongside the work. In a study of kilns in Odisha, a large number of women reported work-related illnesses.

Halima (name changed), from Uttar Pradesh, is at the kiln with four children, including one under a year old. In winter the family of nine lives in a single hut covered with plastic. Children who spend six months at the kiln are cut off from school, and the nearby school teaches in Gujarati, which these families do not speak.
nazar: The system of hiring in pairs and keeping accounts by word of mouth dissolves a woman's labour into the family's labour and makes it vanish. Until every worker's name is recorded separately and payment goes straight into their own account, equal pay for equal work will remain just a slogan.

Labour bound by advances is simply a new form of bonded labour. It is the labour department's responsibility to ensure written accounts, basic facilities and schooling for migrant children at the kilns.
sawal: Where is the name recorded of the woman who moulds the city's bricks?
ref: Jodi
The unit in which workers are hired at kilns, usually a husband and wife. Wages are set per pair and often go in the man's name.
Advance and settlement
An advance taken from the contractor before the season, which is deducted from total earnings at the end when accounts are settled. With verbal accounts, the worker often ends up still in debt.

h: The Friendship Files: a friendship that changed the map of a country
dek: This Hindi documentary by Shadow Citizens begins in post-2002 Gujarat and follows the partnership of a politician and an industrialist, from Mundra port to airports, coal mines and the media.
body: This film runs on one question: can a country's politics and its market be changed on the strength of a single friendship? This documentary by Shadow Citizens looks at the relationship between Narendra Modi and Gautam Adani through that lens.

The story begins in Gujarat after the 2002 riots. According to the film, this was the period when the country's big industrialists were keeping their distance from the state government, and the foundation was laid for a new partnership between politics and business.

From there the film moves to the expansion of Mundra port, then to the years after 2014, when the Adani Group won contracts for six major airports at once, acquired coal mines and power plants, and finally reached a media house like NDTV.

The film's emphasis is not on any one deal but on the decisions and changed rules it sees as the steps of this journey. Its argument is that when rules start being changed to fit one player, it becomes less business and more a part of power.
The Adani Group and the government have consistently rejected such allegations, calling it a story of open bidding and national development. The film leaves this other side for the viewer to weigh.
nazar: The debate on crony capitalism often gets tangled in figures and court papers. This film gives it the shape of a story that an ordinary viewer can follow and understand from start to finish.

The question is not about one businessman. When ports, airports, power and news all start to concentrate in a few hands, the loss falls on the ordinary citizen who has neither the means to bid nor a platform to ask questions.
sawal: When the government and the biggest businessman look in the same direction, whose job is it to ask questions?
ref: Mundra port
The Adani Group's port in Kutch, Gujarat, today considered the country's largest private port.
Shadow Citizens
The name of the team that made this documentary. The film has been put up on the Internet Archive for anyone to watch.

h: Anne Carson: the poet who begins in the middle
dek: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature has gone to Canadian poet Anne Carson. Tribhuvan's long essay reads her world alongside the Hindi and Urdu tradition.
body: This year the Nobel speculation was about Murakami, Gerald Murnane and Thomas Pynchon, but the prize went to Anne Carson, whom the Swedish Academy chose for shaping new literary forms while playing with the classical tradition. Tribhuvan's essay opens with a scene: drinking tea in Reykjavik, Carson does not pick up the phone, her husband does, and rather than celebrate she would prefer a walk in the woods.

The writer picks up Carson's advice to begin writing in the middle and links it to Horace and Homer. He then recalls the Punjabi poet Pash, for whom 'the middle path' is the name of cowardly neutrality. For Carson, the middle means that life, love and memory have no clear beginning or end.

The essay moves through her books. 'Eros the Bittersweet' (1986) rests on Sappho's word in which love is both sweet and bitter, and the writer sets it beside the longing of separation in Vidyapati, Sur, Mahadevi and Mir and Ghalib. In translating Sappho's fragments, Carson leaves the gaps empty, which raises the question of how many voices of folk singers and Dalit women were lost in the same way.

In 'Autobiography of Red', Geryon, the red-winged monster killed by Herakles, becomes a sensitive boy. The writer carefully recalls Shambuka, Eklavya and Karna, and compares it with Dharamvir Bharati's 'Andha Yug' (The Blind Age) and Kunwar Narayan's 'Atmajayi' (Self-Conqueror). The question is whether retelling a myth changes only the words, or the speaker too.

The writer places 'Nox', written on her brother's death, alongside Nirala's 'Saroj Smriti' (In Memory of Saroj), and goes on to 'Glass Essay', 'Decreation' and 'Antigonick'. According to the writer, Carson does not flee from tradition; she finds the ground for experiment within it.
nazar: Writing such a deep reading, rooted in Hindi soil, within a day of the Nobel announcement is a big thing in itself. The essay shows that the best way to read world literature is to carry one's own tradition along, not to set it aside.
sawal: Does retelling a myth give a voice to the defeated?
ref: Sappho
A Greek poet from the island of Lesbos, about six hundred years before Christ, whose poems survive mostly in fragments.
Saroj Smriti
Nirala's long elegy, which he wrote after the death of his daughter Saroj.

h: '27 Down': a forgotten film on the tracks
dek: Arvind Das points out that talk of parallel cinema often leaves out Awtar Kaul's only film, which was based on a Hindi novel.
body: In discussions of Hindi parallel cinema, the names of Mani Kaul and Kumar Shahani come up first. Arvind Das draws attention to the 1973 film '27 Down', based on Ramesh Bakshi's novel 'Atharah Suraj ke Paudhe' (Eighteen Sun Plants). Its director, Awtar Kaul, drowned on the very day the film's National Award was announced. It is his only complete film.

One basis of the essay is Vinod Kaul's book on Awtar Kaul. The writer explains that around 1969 a new wave began with low-budget, literature-based films such as 'Uski Roti', 'Bhuvan Shome' and 'Sara Akash', and that this film was made for about two lakh rupees with a loan from the Film Finance Corporation. Raakhee worked without a fee, without make-up, in a sari from home.

The film's hero, Sanjay, is a railway ticket checker who drifts aimlessly in the shadow of a domineering father. Shalini is a typist in Bombay who carries the burden of her siblings and grandfather and makes her own decisions, quite unlike the Hindi heroines of that time. It was shot with a handheld camera on moving trains, and A K Bir won a National Award for his first film.

The second part is the writer's conversation with M K Raina, for whom this was his first film. Raina recalls Awtar and Bakshi coming to meet him at the NSD hostel; he read the novel in one night, and they talked about the image of the tracks that run together but never meet.

According to Raina, parallel cinema weakened when big stars began to be cast. He believes that Sanjay's restlessness is alive today among young people in small towns, and that if state governments back new filmmakers, cinema can live again.
nazar: Today, when people lament the lack of stories in Hindi films, this essay is a reminder that once a Hindi novel and a government loan together could make such cinema. The question is where that door is for a new filmmaker today.
sawal: Could a new filmmaker today make '27 Down' for two lakh rupees?
ref: Film Finance Corporation
A government body set up in 1960 that gave loans to low-budget experimental films. It later merged into the NFDC.
Awtar Kaul
A filmmaker who lived from 1939 to 1974, whose '27 Down' was also honoured at Locarno and Mannheim.

h: Champaran, where Gandhi became the Mahatma
dek: A report on the launch of Shuja Gandhi's book 'Mitti Yaad Rakhti Hai' (The Soil Remembers), in which a son of Champaran also recalls the Gandhi of his childhood.
body: On the evening before Gandhi Jayanti, 1 October, Shuja Gandhi's book 'Mitti Yaad Rakhti Hai' was launched at Jawahar Bhawan in New Delhi. Published by Pankti Prakashan, the book is about Champaran. Musharraf Parvez's report weaves his own memories into the event.

The writer of the report grew up in Muhammadpur village in Champaran. As a child, Gandhi for him was the man because of whom there was a holiday, and about whom the village's general knowledge questions were asked. He came to know Gandhi seriously by reading 'The Story of My Experiments with Truth'. He also tells the story of foreign tourists he met at the Red Fort who, on hearing the name Champaran, at once called it Gandhi's place.

On the stage were Vijay Mahajan, K L Sharma and Supriya Shrinate. The writer was bothered that the launch of a Hindi book began in English, when Gandhi gave the mother tongue so much respect. Shuja Gandhi said he was born in Champaran and that the region, with its stories and history, is far more than people know.

K L Sharma spoke of indigo cultivation and Kasturba's ashram and said Gandhi saw the deepest poverty in Champaran. Supriya Shrinate called Champaran a symbol of shared strength, where the foundation of the freedom struggle was laid. Vijay Mahajan mentioned his eighty-day journey of 2011, in which he found Champaran and Madurai the most important.
The report ends with a glimpse of the book's first chapter, which begins with the Gandak river: a young, restless river coming down from the Nepal Terai, entering Champaran at Triveni.
nazar: The most honest thing in the report is its complaint about language. At events held in Gandhi's name, Gandhi's own ideas are often the first to be dropped. It should also be noted that all the speakers on stage were linked to the same party, so the book's real test will be among its readers.
sawal: Why launch a Hindi book on Gandhi in English?
ref: Champaran Satyagraha
Gandhi's first major satyagraha in India, in 1917 in Champaran, Bihar, against forced indigo cultivation.
Tinkathia
The system under which farmers had to grow indigo on three kattha (a local land unit) out of every twenty.

h: The science fiction writer and the dark forest of literature
dek: Pragya Gautam's piece, half memoir and half allegory, shows how the Hindi literary world treats science fiction.
body: Pragya Gautam writes science fiction, and this piece opens not like a straight essay but like a dream. The narrator is running through a dark forest, chased by the characters of her unfinished stories, which she threw away one night in anger.

At the root of this unease is a question: who knows you here? Her stories have reached German and Chinese magazines, but no one in her own city recognises her. She pays a fee of two thousand rupees to join a local WhatsApp literary group, where the same faces are honoured at every event and she is advised to give up science fiction and write something else.

At a library event her name was printed on the invitation as a special guest, but others took over the stage and she sat at the back. The writer also mentions an old editor who advised her to promote herself, and with whom she broke off after his improper behaviour, even though it closed the road to awards.

A professor's remark stings her: in the world of literature, science fiction writers have the status of untouchables. One editor puts her off four times but never says no. A writer friend promises a review, stays silent for five months, and when reminded asks whether he is being pressured.

In the end, burning with fever in the summer heatwave, the narrator tears up her old stories and scolds the characters for being too timid. Now they take off their masks and run after her, and the forest is still dense.
nazar: This piece is a mirror of Hindi literary culture, where connections count for more than the work and some genres are treated as second-rate from birth. A language that gives no room to science fiction loses a big tool for thinking about the future.
sawal: Why is science fiction treated as second-rate in Hindi?
ref: Science fiction
Fiction that imagines from the possibilities of science and technology. In Hindi its tradition goes back to the early twentieth century.

h: Eighteen poems for Teejan Bai
dek: Rajendra Sharma's poems bid farewell to the voice of Pandavani that gave Draupadi of the Mahabharata her own tongue.
body: Sammukh has published a series of eighteen short poems by Rajendra Sharma, a tribute to the Pandavani singer Teejan Bai. The poet is from Saharanpur; he retired this year after thirty-nine years in Uttar Pradesh's tax department, and has written steadily on art and music. At the heart of these poems is the thought that Teejan has gone, but her voice has not.

The early poems are about Teejan's bond with SPIC MACAY, which she called her maika (mother's home). Thirty years together, performances from city to city, and her last stage, in Jodhpur in 2023, are recorded in them. One poem captures the moment when the organisation's founder, though older than her, touches her feet.

The most moving poems are about the difference between Teejan behind the stage and on it. A frail old woman in a wheelchair, nervously twisting the end of her sari, who becomes almost a goddess as soon as she steps into the light, and turns humble again the moment the song ends.

Several poems answer the criticism that Pandavani is a men's style. According to the poet, Teejan gave this tradition a woman's body and the restlessness of an era, and through Draupadi gave a voice to every silenced woman. In one poem Draupadi, Bhima, Karna and Arjuna themselves mourn: who will tell their story now?

The last poems speak of the immersion of her ashes at the Sangam, the silent ektara (one-stringed instrument), and a Chhattisgarh that does not weep but mourns like a mother proud of her daughter's success. Go to Sammukh to read the poems in full.
nazar: These poems do not claim to be great poetry; they are a listener's gratitude. But they hold something important: the real legacy of a folk art lies not in one artist but in the thousands of voices that sing after her.
sawal: After Teejan, whose hands hold the torch of Pandavani?
ref: Pandavani
A folk singing style of Chhattisgarh in which a performer with a tambura or ektara narrates the story of the Mahabharata through song and acting.
Kapalik style
The style of Pandavani in which the performer stands and tells the story dramatically. Teejan Bai was its defining face.

h: Puppetry: folk memory tied to strings
dek: Akhilesh Kumar Maurya's essay explores the puppetry tradition from Rajasthan to Andhra and from Japan to Indonesia, and asks how it can survive.
body: The word kathputli comes from kath (wood) and putli (doll), but the writer points out that these dolls have also been made of cloth, paper, leather and clay. What really brings them to life is the artist's voice, music and storytelling. The essay begins with a story of Shiva and Parvati and goes on to the sutradhar of the Natyashastra, a word linked to the one who moves characters by a string.

In the time of the Bhakti movement, when reading and writing were rare in villages, puppet shows carried religious stories to ordinary people. In Rajasthan the Bhat community preserved this art for generations and told the ballads of Pabuji and Amar Singh Rathore with string puppets.

The writer lists the variety across the country: Andhra's leather shadow puppetry, tholu bommalata; Odisha's kathi kandhei; Bengal's putul nach; limited use in Assam's bhaona; and figures of wood and straw in the rituals of the Gond, Baiga and Santhal communities of central India. Around the world, Japan's bunraku and Indonesia's wayang kulit belong to the same family.

In the colonial era puppet shows satirised social evils and the administration, and after independence they carried messages of literacy, sanitation and women's rights to villages. They are also an effective medium in children's education and special education.

The trouble is that television and mobile phones have taken away audiences, uncertain earnings keep young people away, and performance spaces in cities are shrinking. The writer names digital platforms, a place in the school curriculum and financial support for artists as the way ahead.
nazar: The essay is a good introduction, but the real question is the one that comes at the end: what of the livelihood of the families who carried this art for centuries? Every plan to save culture is incomplete until the artist's poverty is at its centre.
sawal: If puppetry is to be saved, who will save the puppeteers?
ref: Tholu bommalata
Shadow puppetry of Andhra Pradesh, in which coloured leather figures are shown on a screen with the help of light.
Wayang kulit
Indonesia's tradition of leather shadow puppetry, recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage.

h: Anand Teltumbde: Jantar Mantar must not become a graveyard of movements
dek: The noted thinker warns that the cockroach movement's strength lies in being unpredictable, not in one face or one fixed place.
body: Anand Teltumbde's essay first appeared in Frontline and was later published in Hindi on Workers Unity. He begins with the remark in which, it is alleged, unemployed young people were called cockroaches. The remark was insulting, he says, but it revealed a mindset in which citizens are merely subjects to be managed. Abhijeet Dipke's achievement was to turn the insult into a basis for solidarity.

The writer accepts that the anger of the young is justified, but he sees paper leaks, recruitment scams and flawed evaluations as symptoms of a deeper illness: weakening public institutions, education for sale and politics of spectacle. Removing one minister or official does not change that structure.

His sharpest point is about Jantar Mantar. According to Teltumbde, the government has turned it into a place where protest is allowed but cannot touch the working of government. The police, TV channels and parties have learnt to manage it, so movements there often end up as rituals. In his view it is less a birthplace of movements and more a graveyard.

He considers the CJP's demands reformist rather than transformative, and warns that Dipke could become the next Arvind Kejriwal, an outsider whom the system absorbed. The strength of the youth movements in Bangladesh and Nepal, he says, was that they moved faster than the government could prepare and reached places no one expected. A movement with a fixed date, a fixed place and a demand for resignation is easy to read.

The path he suggests is slow: no headquarters, no supreme leader, and building networks among colleges, factories, villages and informal workers. Linking unemployment with paper leaks, the farm crisis with democratic decline, communal tension with economic hardship. He leaves the question open: will the cockroaches prove as stubborn as their name, or become just a memory like earlier movements?
nazar: The essay was written before today, but what happened in Delhi today was like a test of it. Nobody could reach Jantar Mantar, and leaders said: wherever you are stopped, make that your Jantar Mantar. Sit-ins at police stations, slogans in buses, groups scattered across the city: perhaps without meaning to, the movement is showing the very unpredictability Teltumbde talks about. The real test now is whether, after Monday, this anger reaches colleges and neighbourhoods or stays confined to TV studios.
sawal: Who can stop a movement that has no single face?
ref: Anand Teltumbde
Writer, civil rights activist and management professor; author of more than 30 books on caste and democracy.
Jantar Mantar
The road near Parliament in New Delhi that has for years been the designated place for sit-ins and protests.

h: Manage, don't block: the 2012 lesson for the Home Ministry
dek: A security affairs journalist argues that if Delhi Police had been allowed to talk to the protesters, the whole city would not have become a cantonment.
body: Namrata Biji Ahuja asks whether refusing permission at Jantar Mantar on 10 October, imposing Section 163 and bringing in paramilitary forces was necessary, and whether the Home Ministry should have taken charge directly. Her answer is clear: this is the job of Delhi Police, which should have agreed the place, time and conditions with the protesters.

She recalls 2012, when after the Nirbhaya case crowds reached North Block. The Home Secretary then handed the Police Commissioner the job of handling the situation, the government drafted an ordinance overnight that later became law, and the ministry stayed out of the political fight. The street stayed with the police, the decisions with the policymakers.

In the article, security officials, unnamed, express surprise that this time the Home Secretary himself is leading and writing letters to states. They accept that the 2012 movement was not political in this way, but say the ministry should trust officers' experience rather than weigh the nature of the protest. If orders from above come before negotiation, the police are left only to enforce restrictions and protesters do not even know where they may gather.

Yashovardhan Azad, former special director of the IB, gives the example of London, where the police chief allowed a pro-Palestine demonstration despite political objections, because there was no firm fear of disorder. According to the article, the IB's job is to report ground conditions, not to watch the opposition, and confusion over information made room for excessive harshness.

In the end the writer says the way forward is for the police and the IB to do their jobs, and for the ministry to stop reacting directly to every protest that reaches its door. The lesson is that a strategy to manage movements is needed, not to stop them.
nazar: This piece is written not from a left perspective but from voices inside the security system, and that is why it matters. When former officers themselves say such harshness was not needed, the question becomes less about law and order and more about political intent. Thousands of detentions, closed metro stations and cancelled trains look like the result not of any threat but of avoiding dialogue. The only difference is that in 2012 the government listened to the demand; this time it is counting the crowd.
sawal: Why does the government shy away from talking to protesters?
ref: Section 163, BNSS
The section of the new criminal procedure code under which authorities can ban gatherings in an area; it replaced the old Section 144.
The 2012 Nirbhaya movement
A nationwide movement after a gang rape in Delhi, after which laws on sexual violence were made stricter.
